title: ⭐⭐ Revision: from the map to the microphone

questions.prompt: A brochure writer types this line: "Loch Ness is the most famous." Her editor sends it back and tells her that one thing is missing. What must she add?

options.text: a second adjective beside the first one: the most famous and beautiful lake
the word very in front of it, as in the very most famous lake of all
an ordinal number before it, as in the second most famous lake there is
the group she compares it with, as in the most famous lake in Britain

questions.explanation: A superlative sets one thing against a group, and until the group is named the sentence has said nothing: the most famous of what? The range comes in with in (in Britain, in the world), with of (of the three, of them all) or with a relative clause (that I have ever seen), and one of the three is compulsory. Adding a second adjective only doubles the same hole. Very is refused outright, because the superlative is already the top and English does not push it further. And an ordinal changes the claim instead of completing it: the second most famous still needs its range, and it now says that one lake is ahead.

questions.prompt: A visitor tells her friends: "I meant to spend ten minutes in that little museum and I came out two hours later." Which adjective of this lesson names exactly what the museum did to her?

options.text: breathtaking
magnificent
captivating
splendid

questions.explanation: Captivating means holding somebody the way a captor holds a prisoner: you cannot leave, and the ten minutes become two hours without your noticing. That is precisely the story she tells. Breathtaking is about a single second, not about two hours — it names the view that stops your breath as you turn the corner. Magnificent is about size and grandeur, and this museum is little. Splendid is warm general praise that would fit anything at all, which is why it says the least of the four. These words look interchangeable in a dictionary and are not: each one names the effect it describes.

questions.prompt: A tourist office has written a paragraph that gives the town's position on the coast, the number of people who live there, and the days its market opens. There is not one word of praise in it. What is that paragraph written to do?

options.text: to persuade: it pushes the reader to come and see the town
to inform: it puts checkable facts in front of the reader
to narrate: it tells the story of the town in order of time
to argue: it defends the writer's own opinion of the town

questions.explanation: Three facts, all of them checkable, and not one adjective of praise: that is a text written to inform, and it is the purpose of the text about Edinburgh in your book. Persuading would turn towards the reader with an imperative and a promise, and the word of praise the writer has carefully not used is exactly the tool it would need. Narrating puts events in the order they happened, and nothing here happens. And arguing defends an opinion, which needs an owner — an I think or a to me — that no line of this paragraph has. Ask the same question of every document you meet: is it here to inform me, to move me, or to tell me a story?

questions.prompt: The pronunciation box of this lesson puts "north" and "south" on one line and "northern" and "southern" on the next. What does adding the ending -ern change?

options.text: the th: it becomes the voiced th heard in the word the
nothing in the sound: only the spelling gets longer
the vowel only: it becomes longer, and the th stays put
the stress: it moves onto the last part of the word

questions.explanation: English has two th sounds. North and south end in the one with no voice in it, the th of three and thin; add -ern and the throat starts buzzing, so northern and southern take the th of the and this. Put your fingers on your throat and say the two words one after the other — you will feel the difference before you hear it. The spelling gives no warning at all, which is why the box exists. And southern hides a second change: its vowel shrinks from the /aʊ/ of south to a short /ʌ/, so the word ends up sounding much shorter than it looks.

questions.prompt: A ferry company's small print says: "Free delivery anywhere in Great Britain." A customer who lives in Belfast is charged for her delivery and complains. Is the company entitled to charge her?

options.text: No: Northern Ireland is a part of Great Britain, like Wales.
No: Great Britain and the United Kingdom are two names for one country.
Yes: Belfast is in the Republic of Ireland, a separate country.
Yes: Belfast is in the United Kingdom, but not on Great Britain.

questions.explanation: The small print names an island, and Belfast is not on it: the city stands in Northern Ireland, on the island of Ireland, and the free delivery therefore stops at the water. Northern Ireland is nonetheless fully inside the United Kingdom, so the company would have had to pay if its own line had said anywhere in the UK — which is why the two names are never interchangeable in a contract. And Belfast is not in the Republic of Ireland: the border between the two runs across the island. This is what the distinction is for. It is not a piece of trivia, it is the difference between paying and not paying.

questions.prompt: A palace is described as the official residence of a head of state. Which sentence follows from those two words?

options.text: It is the only house he may own for as long as he holds office.
It is a museum that carries his name, open to the public all year.
It is the house that his post gives him, not one he bought.
It is the house he was born in, and his family still lives there.

questions.explanation: Official means belonging to the post and not to the person: the house comes with the job, the head of state lives in it while he holds the job, and he moves out when somebody else takes over. He never bought it and he does not own it, so nothing here limits what he may own elsewhere. A residence is a home, not a museum, however many visitors are let in on a Sunday. And a birthplace is exactly what an official residence is not — that would be a private house, with no post attached to it. Put former in front of the pair and you get the third fact of the family: he used to live there and does not now.
